Main.sentence: Somerville ( /ˈsʌmərvɪl/ ___E:SUM-ər-vil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key)___ ) is a city located directly to the northwest of ___E:Boston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston)___ , and north of ___E:Cambridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts)___ , in ___E:Middlesex County, Massachusetts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesex_County,_Massachusetts)___ , United States.
As of the ___E:2020 United States census U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census)___ , the city had a total population of 81,045 people.

With an area of 4.12 square miles (10.7 km 2 ), the city has a density of 19,671/sq mi (7,595/km 2 ), making it the most densely populated municipality in ___E:New England U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England)___ and the ___E:19th most densely populated incorporated municipality in the country U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_cities_by_population_density)___ .
Somerville was established as a town in 1842, when it was separated from ___E:Charlestown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlestown,_Massachusetts)___ .
In 2006, the city was named the best-run city in Massachusetts by The Boston Globe .
In 1972, 2009, and 2015, the city received the ___E:All-America City Award U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-America_City_Award)___ .

It is home to ___E:Tufts University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tufts_University)___ , which has its campus along the Somerville and ___E:Medford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medford,_Massachusetts)___ border.

Tufts, alongside ___E:Harvard University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University)___ and the ___E:Massachusetts Institute of Technology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology)___ , makes up one corner of the Brain Power Triangle, which thus includes the city of Somerville.

The area that would become Somerville was inhabited for thousands of years prior to ___E:European colonization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_colonization_of_the_Americas)___ , with multiple archaeological sites indicating habitation in the ___E:Mystic River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystic_River)___ watershed as early as the beginning of the ___E:Archaic Period U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaic_period_(North_America))___ (8000–1000 BCE).

At the time of English contact in the 1600s, the Somerville area was inhabited by the Mystic Tribe of the ___E:Naumkeag people U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naumkeag_people)___ , headed by the ___E:Squaw Sachem U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squaw_Sachem_of_Mistick)___ and her son ___E:Wonohaquaham U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonohaquaham)___ .

Though no archaeological sites within Somerville have been identified from this time period, an indigenous settlement near College Hill in Somerville can be inferred from contemporary written records.
The Mystic River continued to be an important regional core for the Naumkeag into the period of European colonization in the 16th and 17th centuries.
In 1627, Mystic ___E:sachem U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sachem)___ Wonohaquaham reportedly gave permission for English settlement at Charlestown,  which then included present-day Somerville.
In 1639, his mother the Squaw Sachem deeded the land that would become Somerville to English settlers.
The territory now comprising the city of Somerville was first settled by Europeans in 1629 as part of ___E:Charlestown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlestown,_Massachusetts)___ .

In 1629, English surveyor ___E:Thomas Graves U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Graves_(engineer))___ led a scouting party of 100 ___E:Puritans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puritans)___ from the settlement of ___E:Salem U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salem,_Massachusetts)___ to prepare the site for the ___E:Great Migration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Migration_(Puritan))___ of ___E:Puritans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puritans)___ from ___E:England U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England)___ .

Graves was attracted to the narrow Mishawum Peninsula between the ___E:Charles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_River)___ and ___E:Mystic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystic_River)___ rivers, linked to the mainland at the present-day ___E:Sullivan Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sullivan_Square)___ .

The area of earliest settlement was based at City Square on the peninsula, though the territory of Charlestown officially included all of what is now Somerville, as well as ___E:Medford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medford,_Massachusetts)___ , ___E:Everett U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everett,_Massachusetts)___ , ___E:Malden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malden,_Massachusetts)___ ,  ___E:Stoneham U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoneham,_Massachusetts)___ ,  ___E:Melrose U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melrose,_Massachusetts)___ , ___E:Woburn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woburn,_Massachusetts)___ , ___E:Burlington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_Massachusetts)___ , and parts of ___E:Arlington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Massachusetts)___ and ___E:Cambridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts)___ .

From that time until 1842, the area of present-day Somerville was referred to as "beyond the Neck" in reference to the thin spit of land, the ___E:Charlestown Neck U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlestown_Neck)___ , that connected it to the Charlestown Peninsula.
The first European settler in Somerville of whom there is any record was John Woolrich, an Indian trader who came from the Charlestown Peninsula in 1630, and settled near what is now Dane Street.
Others soon followed Woolrich, locating in the vicinity of present-day ___E:Union Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Square_(Somerville))___ .
In 1639 colonists officially acquired the land in what is now Somerville from the ___E:Squaw Sachem of Mistick U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squaw_Sachem_of_Mistick)___ .
The population continued to slowly increase, and by 1775 there were about 500 inhabitants scattered across the area. Otherwise, the area was mostly used as grazing and farmland.
It was once known as the "Stinted Pasture" or "Cow Commons", as early settlers of Charlestown had the right to pasture a certain number of cows in the area.

___E:John Winthrop U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Winthrop)___ , the first colonial governor of the ___E:Massachusetts Bay Colony U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony)___ , was granted 600 acres (240 hectares) of land in the area in 1631. Named for the ten small knolls located on the property, Ten Hills Farm extended from the Cradock Bridge in present-day Medford Square to Convent Hill in ___E:East Somerville U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Somerville)___ .

Winthrop lived, planted, and raised cattle on the farm. It is also where he launched the first ship in Massachusetts, the " ___E:Blessing of the Bay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blessing_of_the_Bay)___ ".
Built for trading purposes in the early 1630s, it was soon armed for use as a patrol boat for the New England coast.
It is seen as a precursor to the ___E:United States Navy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy)___ .
The " ___E:Ten Hills U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ten_Hills)___ " neighborhood, located in the northeastern part of the city, has retained the name for over 300 years.

New research has found that less than a decade after John Winthrop moved to the farm in 1631, there were enslaved Native American ___E:prisoners of war U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoners_of_war)___ on the property.
Each successive owner of Ten Hills Farm would depend upon slavery's profits until the 1780s, when Massachusetts abolished the practice.

In a short time, the settlers began laying out roads in all directions in search of more land for planting and trade with various Native American tribes in the area. Laid out as early as the mid-1630s, the earliest highway in Somerville was probably what is now Washington Street, and led from present-day Sullivan Square to ___E:Harvard Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Square)___ .
In its earliest days, Washington Street was known as the "Road to Newtowne" (renamed Cambridge in 1638).

During the 1700s and early 1800s Somerville Avenue was "Milk Row," a route favored by ___E:Middlesex County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesex_County,_Massachusetts)___ dairy farmers as the best way to get to the markets of Charlestown and Boston.

Laid out in 1636, Broadway was likely the second highway built in the area. Originally called "Menotomie's Road", it ran from the Charlestown Neck to the settlement at Menotomy (present-day ___E:Arlington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Massachusetts)___ ).
Initially bordered by farmsteads, Broadway would come into its own as a commercial thoroughfare after horse-drawn trolleys were introduced to the highway in 1858.
Somerville was home to one of the first hostile acts of the ___E:American Revolutionary War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War)___ .

The removal of gunpowder by British soldiers from a powder magazine in 1774, and the ___E:massive popular reaction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powder_Alarm)___ that ensued, are considered to be a turning point in the events leading up to war.

First built by settlers for use as a windmill in the early 1700s, the ___E:Old Powder House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Powder_House)___ was sold to the colonial government of Massachusetts for use as a ___E:gunpowder magazine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunpowder_magazine)___ in 1747. Located at the intersection of Broadway and College Avenue in present-day ___E:Powder House Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powder_House_Square)___ , the Old Powder House held the largest supply of gunpowder in all of Massachusetts.

General ___E:Thomas Gage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Gage)___ , who had become the military governor of Massachusetts in May 1774, was charged with enforcement of the highly unpopular ___E:Intolerable Acts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intolerable_Acts)___ , which ___E:British Parliament U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Great_Britain)___ had passed in response to the ___E:Boston Tea Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Tea_Party)___ .

Seeking to prevent the outbreak of war, he believed that the best way to accomplish this was by secretly removing military stores from storehouses and arsenals in ___E:New England U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England)___ .

Just after dawn on September 1, 1774, a force of roughly 260 British ___E:regulars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_army)___ from the ___E:4th Regiment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Own_Royal_Regiment_(Lancaster))___ , under the command of Lieutenant Colonel George Maddison, were rowed in secrecy up the ___E:Mystic River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystic_River)___ from ___E:Boston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston,_Massachusetts)___ to a landing point near Winter Hill. From there they marched about one mile (1.5 kilometers) to the Powder House, and after sunrise removed all of the gunpowder.

Most of the regulars then returned to Boston the way they had come, but a small contingent marched on to ___E:Cambridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts)___ , seizing two ___E:field pieces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Artillery)___ from the ___E:Cambridge Common U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Common)___ .

The field pieces and powder were then taken from Boston to the British stronghold on ___E:Castle Island U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Island_(Massachusetts))___ , then known as Castle William (renamed ___E:Fort Independence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Independence_(Massachusetts))___ in 1779).

In response to the raid, amid rumors that blood had been shed, alarm spread through the countryside as far as ___E:Connecticut U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut_Colony)___ and beyond, and ___E:American Patriots U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriot_(American_Revolution))___ sprang into action, fearing that war was at hand. Thousands of militiamen began streaming toward ___E:Boston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston)___ and ___E:Cambridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts)___ , and mob action forced ___E:Loyalists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyalist_(American_Revolution))___ and some government officials to flee to the protection of the ___E:British Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army)___ .

This action provided a "dress rehearsal" for the ___E:Battles of Lexington and Concord U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battles_of_Lexington_and_Concord)___ seven months later in the famous "shot heard 'round the world", and inflamed already heated feelings on both sides, spurring actions by both British and American forces to remove powder and cannon to secure locations.
After the raid on the Powder House, the colonists took action to conceal arms and munitions of war in ___E:Concord U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord,_Massachusetts)___ .
When General Gage found out, he was resolved to take the powder by force if necessary.

The Americans learned that the British intended to start for Concord on April 18, 1775, and couriers ___E:Paul Revere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Revere)___ and ___E:William Dawes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Dawes)___ set out on their famous ride to warn the farmers and militiamen in between Boston and Concord, including ___E:Sam Adams U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Adams)___ and ___E:John Hancock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hancock)___ .

That night, he set out from the ___E:North End U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_End,_Boston)___ through ___E:Charlestown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlestown,_Boston)___ towards ___E:East Somerville U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Somerville)___ .
In Revere's own written account of his ride, he mentions a specific location in Somerville (then part of Charlestown).

The location was the site where the executed body of a local enslaved man known as " ___E:Mark U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Codman)___ ", owned by John Codman, was publicly ___E:gibbeted U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbet)___ and displayed for several years after his execution.
The location is probably near the site of the present day Holiday Inn on Washington Street.
Revere wrote "nearly opposite where Mark was hung in chains, I saw two men on Horse back, under a Tree",  which he then realized were two British officers stationed on Washington Street.

They immediately pursued him, and Revere galloped up Broadway towards Winter Hill and eventually eluded them. His warning gave the militia enough time to prepare for battle, and launch the American Revolution.

Shortly after Paul Revere set out on his ride, Lieutenant Colonel ___E:Francis Smith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Smith_(British_Army_officer))___ and 700 British Army regulars landed near ___E:Lechmere Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lechmere_Square)___ .

As it was nearly high tide, ___E:East Cambridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Cambridge)___ was an island and the troops, skirting the marshes, were obliged to wade "thigh deep" to reach Somerville.
They probably came through Prospect Street into Washington Street, and through Union Square.
Defeated and in retreat, the British army passed again through Somerville en route back to Boston.
Upon reaching Union Square, the British marched down Washington Street as far as the base of Prospect Hill, where a skirmish took place.
The handful of rebellious locals, having heard of the storied battles at Lexington and Concord earlier that day, caught an exhausted retreating British contingent off guard.
As the story goes, 65-year-old minuteman James Miller lost his life in the scuffle while standing his ground against the British.
He was shot thirteen times after famously telling a retreating colleague, "I am too old to run."

Somerville occupied a conspicuous position during the entire ___E:Siege of Boston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Boston)___ , which lasted nine months, and Prospect Hill became the central position of the ___E:Continental Army's U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Army)___ chain of emplacements north of Boston.
Its height and commanding view of Boston and the harbor had tremendous strategic value and the fortress became known as the "Citadel".

Originally occupied by just 400 men, Prospect Hill became a primary encampment for American forces after General ___E:Israel Putnam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Putnam)___ 's retreat from the ___E:Battle of Bunker Hill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bunker_Hill)___ .

It is believed that on January 1, 1776, the ___E:Continental Union Flag U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Union_Flag)___ flew for the first time at the Citadel, the first official raising of an American flag.
With the Revolutionary War over, the residents of Somerville were able once again to devote their energies wholeheartedly to the business of making a living.

From the 1780s until Somerville's separation from Charlestown in 1842, material progress was continuous, if a bit slow. As transportation infrastructure gradually transformed the area, new industries sprang up, such as brickmaking, quarrying and dairy farming.

Transportation improvements in the early to mid-1800s factored significantly in the growth of a more urban residential form and Somerville's incorporation as a City in 1872. These improvements included the opening of the ___E:Middlesex Canal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesex_Canal)___ through Somerville in 1803,  various turnpikes such as Medford and Beacon streets, built during the 1810s and 1820s, and especially the introduction of rail lines.

In 1841, the ___E:Fitchburg Railroad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitchburg_Railroad)___ was built between Boston and ___E:Fresh Pond U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresh_Pond_(Cambridge,_Massachusetts))___ in Cambridge, paralleling the route of Somerville Avenue.

This led to the establishment of industries along its path. Soon after, in 1843 the Fitchburg Railroad commenced passenger service and enabled residential development along the southern slopes of Prospect and Spring hills.
By the early 1840s, the population of present-day Somerville topped 1,000 for the first time.
Despite the growth, however, discontent was growing steadily outside the "neck".
The area's rural farmers paid taxes to the local government in Charlestown, but received little in return.
By 1842, the area had no churches, few schools, no taverns, and suffered from poor and impassable roads.
For many years after the Revolution the two parts of Charlestown styled "within" and "without the neck" were nearly equal in population; the former had by this time completely outstripped the latter.
With this growth of population and trade came the need of city institutions, and consequently greater expenses were involved.

Therefore, the rural part of Charlestown found itself contributing to the paving of the streets, the maintenance of a night watch, to the building of engine houses, and various other improvements from which they derived little benefit.

In 1828, a petition was presented to the ___E:Legislature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_General_Court)___ asking that a part of Charlestown be set off as a separate town, to be known as Warren.
This petition was subsequently withdrawn.

The desire for a separate township continued to spread, and by 1841, becoming impatient at the neglect of the government to adequately provide for their needs, the inhabitants again agitated a division of the town, and a meeting in reference to the matter was held November 22 in the Prospect Hill school house.
A petition was accordingly drawn up and signed by Guy C. Hawkins and 151 others, and a committee deputed to further its passage through the legislature, then in session.

A bill ___E:incorporating U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_(United_States_Census_Bureau))___ a new town was signed by the governor on March 3, 1842. The original choice for the city's new name, after breaking away from Charlestown, was Walford, after the first settler of Charlestown, Thomas Walford.
However, this name was not adopted by the separation committee.
Charles Miller, a member of this committee, proposed the name "Somerville", which was ultimately chosen.
It was not derived from any one person's name, and a report commissioned by the Somerville Historical Society found that Somerville was a "purely fanciful name".
Before Somerville became a township in 1842 the area was primarily populated by British farmers and brick makers who sold their wares in the markets of Boston, Cambridge and Charlestown.

As the markets grew, the population of Somerville increased six-fold between the years of 1842 and 1870 to 14,685. With the sharp influx of immigrants to the Somerville area, industry boomed and brick manufacturing became the predominant trade.

Before mechanical presses were invented, Somerville produced 1.3 million bricks a year. Thereafter, production increased rapidly to 5.5 million bricks a year, and the success of the brickyards began to attract numerous other industries.
In 1851, American Tubes Works opened, followed by meat processing and packaging plants.
Other Somerville factories came to produce steam engines, boilers, household appliances, glass, and iron.

Shortly thereafter Somerville incorporated as a city in 1872. The population growth was due in part to improvements in pre-existing transportation lines, as well as a new rail line, the ___E:Lexington and Arlington Railroad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexington_and_Arlington_Railroad)___ , introduced through ___E:Davis Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davis_Square)___ in 1870. At its height, Somerville was served by eight passenger rail stations.
Somerville's buoyant economy during this period was tied to industries that tended to locate at the periphery of the residential core, near freight rail corridors.
By the mid-1870s ___E:meat packing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meat_packing_industry)___ plants were the primary employers and profit centers of the community.
The Late Industrial Period (1870–1915) was a time of phenomenal growth for Somerville in all spheres including civic and commercial ventures.
Infrastructure such as rail, water lines, telegraph and electricity were established and connected to surrounding towns.

The population soared from 15,000 to 90,000. While brickmaking had taken a hold in the area after the railroads first arrived in the 1830s, Somerville's brickyards boomed through 1870. Meatpacking soon displaced brickmaking as the primary industry in the city, dubbed "The Chicago of New England".
Additionally, Somerville's location adjacent to Boston and proximity to rail and road transportation made it an ideal location for distribution facilities.
It was in this period that Irish immigrants moved to Somerville to work in the brickyards and on the railroad.
At the same time, older residents of East Boston and Charlestown moved to Somerville to seek a more bucolic setting than that of more densely populated areas.

They also worked to maintain political control over immigrant groups, using slogans such as "Keep Somerville Republican" and establishing a local branch of the anti-Catholic ___E:American Protective Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Protective_Association)___ .

Between 1915 and 1930 population growth slowed slightly as Somerville's industries consolidated rather than expanded, and the period's most important enterprises were meat packing, dairy processing, ice and food distribution.
In 1920, 73% of meatpacking in Massachusetts occurred in Somerville.

Construction of the McGrath Highway in 1925 marked the turning point of Somerville as an industrial city, which accelerated when the ___E:Ford Motor Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Motor_Company)___ built ___E:a plant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerville_Assembly)___ in ___E:Assembly Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_Square)___ in 1926. In the years that followed, Somerville would see itself transformed into a major industrial center as automobile assembly surpassed meat packing as Somerville's most important industry.
By 1930, 70% of Somerville residents had either been born outside of the United States or had parents who were. The population was then estimated to be 60% Catholic.

Although Union Square and Davis Square continued to be the largest commercial areas during the first decades of the 20th century, smaller, less-developed squares grew as well. ___E:Ball Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_Square)___ , ___E:Magoun Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magoun_Square)___ and ___E:Teele Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teele_Square)___ were developed with one- or two-story masonry commercial buildings, and the public green at ___E:Gilman Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilman_Square)___ was surrounded by multiple four-story commercial buildings.
Retail development and banking facilities also spread.

During this time of industrial prosperity, continuing through World War II, the city of Somerville reached its population apex at 105,883 residents in 1940. The building boom continued until the 1940s, creating the dense residential fabric the "city of homes" is known for.
By mid-century, powerful social and economic forces precipitated a period of industrial and population decline that lasted into the 1980s.
The postwar period was characterized by the ascent of the private automobile, which carried significant implications for Somerville.

Streetcar lines that had crisscrossed the city since 1890 were systematically ripped out and commuter rail service was discontinued at the city's eight railway stations, one by one. Passenger rail service along the Fitchburg and Lowell lines had been declining for some time, and stations such as the ___E:Winter Hill station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Hill_station)___ at ___E:Gilman Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilman_Square)___ were removed as early as the late 1940s.
Passenger rail service stopped altogether by 1958.
The number of cars on Somerville's streets continued to rise, and road construction projects proliferated.

The ___E:Alewife Brook Parkway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alewife_Brook_Parkway)___ , ___E:Mystic Valley Parkway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystic_Valley_Parkway)___ and the ___E:Fells Connector Parkways U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fells_Connector_Parkways)___ , originally conceived in the 1890s as a means for city residents to reach the metropolitan parks, evolved into congested commuter routes for suburban drivers.

Highway projects were advanced in the wake of the ___E:Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal-Aid_Highway_Act_of_1956)___ , in some instances displacing entire neighborhoods.

The ___E:Brickbottom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brickbottom_(Somerville,_Massachusetts))___ neighborhood was razed in 1950 to prepare for a proposed ___E:Inner Belt Expressway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_695_(Massachusetts))___ , and construction of ___E:Interstate 93 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_93)___ resulted in demolition of homes in The States neighborhood during the late 1960s.
In 1970, the ___E:state authorized rent control U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rent_control_in_Massachusetts)___ in municipalities with more than 50,000 residents.
Somerville, Lynn, Brookline, and Cambridge subsequently adopted rent control.
Rent control was ___E:repealed statewide in 1994 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Massachusetts_elections#Question_9)___ via ballot initiative.
At the time, only Boston, Cambridge, and Brookline had rent control measures in place.

Industry slowly moved outward to the metropolitan fringes, encouraged by highway access and cheap, undeveloped land. ___E:The Ford Motor Plant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerville_Assembly)___ in ___E:Assembly Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_Square)___ , which had been one of the region's largest employers, closed its doors in 1958 with severe consequences for the local economy.

From the late 1950s through the early 1970s, ___E:Finast Supermarkets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finast)___ used the building that had earlier housed the Ford assembly plant on Middlesex Avenue, but in 1976 it too closed its doors.

By 1976, Assembly Square was becoming a ghost town: Finast Stores, the ___E:Boston and Maine Railroad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Maine_Railroad)___ , and Ford Motor Company, which had each paid the city over $1 million in annual taxes, were gone. By the late 1970s, Somerville was losing population, revenue and jobs.
Somerville also has a history of racial tension.

It only hired its first black police officer, a person named Francis Moore, in 1974.  Moore subsequently won a suit charging that the police department was "blatantly discriminatory" against him, including an episode in which he was told to patrol the East Somerville neighborhood of Glen Park at night without his issued ___E:firearm U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidearm_(weapon))___ , night stick, Mace, or communication devices.
Moore's name had been written on a barrel in the neighborhood and used for target practice by local youth.
In the last years of the 20th century, the situation in Somerville stabilized and growth returned—first to West Somerville, and then the rest of the city.

Almost thirty years after passenger rail service to Somerville was halted, the ___E:Red Line U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_(MBTA))___ Northwest Extension reached ___E:Davis Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davis_Square)___ in 1984. The city and community used the creation of the new station as a catalyst for revitalizing the faded square, promoting new commercial development and sponsoring other physical and infrastructural improvements.
However, when the new transit station opened, business around Davis Square did not immediately thrive.
The number of retail stores in the area declined from 68 in 1977 to 56 in 1987.
However many non-retail uses, such as beauty salons and real estate offices, had already begun to fill the empty retail spaces.

With the Boston area's emergence from its long recession, the area truly began to revive. [citation needed] Clearly, [original research?] the community's vision of a rebirth of commercial and retail activity has, in the past few years, [when?] been fully realized. [original research?] All benefit from their proximity to the MBTA station, with connections to Cambridge and Boston. [citation needed] Retail vacancy rates around the square were close to zero as of 2013.
The telecommunication and biotechnology booms of the mid-to-late 1990s significantly contributed to Somerville's revitalization.

As with the housing boom a century earlier, the sudden increase in the number of jobs available in the cities of Somerville, Boston, and particularly Cambridge—as well as in the other communities immediately surrounding Somerville—led to a new surge in the demand for housing.

Additionally, the end of ___E:rent control U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rent_control)___ in Cambridge coincided with the economic recovery in 1995, increasing demand for Somerville's affordable housing options.
The city also had a very high car theft rate, once being the car theft capital of the country, and its Assembly Square area was especially infamous for this.

However, after the ___E:gentrification U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentrification)___ period the city went through in the 1990s, and an influx of artists to the area, this name has mostly faded from use and the city has instead gained a reputation for its active arts community and effective government, including being named the best-run city in Massachusetts in 2006.  Nowadays lobbying by grassroots organizations is attempting to revive and preserve Somerville's "small-town" neighborhood environments by supporting local business, public transit and gardens.

For some Somerville residents, some of these efforts, such as the 2022 ___E:Green Line extensions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_Extension)___ into Somerville, present a challenge for balancing accessibility of public transit and the need for affordable housing.

According to the ___E:United States Census Bureau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau)___ , Somerville has a total area of 4.2 square miles (11 km 2 ), of which 4.1 square miles (11 km 2 ) is land and 0.1 square miles (0.26 km 2 ), or 2.61%, is water.

Somerville is bordered by the cities of ___E:Cambridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts)___ , ___E:Medford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medford,_Massachusetts)___ , ___E:Everett U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everett,_Massachusetts)___ , ___E:Arlington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Massachusetts)___ and the ___E:Boston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston)___ neighborhood of ___E:Charlestown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlestown,_Boston,_Massachusetts)___ .
It is located on the west bank of the ___E:Mystic River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystic_River)___ .
Millennia ago, glaciation left a series of ___E:drumlins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drumlins)___ running west to east across the landscape of what would become Somerville.

These ridges would later become known as the "Seven Hills" of Somerville (like ___E:many other cities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_claimed_to_be_built_on_seven_hills)___ claiming to be built on seven hills, following the ___E:seven hills of Rome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_hills_of_Rome)___ ):

These hills rise from the ___E:floodplain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floodplain)___ of the Mystic River, and generally run west to east, providing views of Boston to the south and Medford/Everett to the north.

Physical boundaries are also defined by prominent waterways: the Mystic River to the north, its tributary ___E:Alewife Brook U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alewife_Brook_Reservation)___ to the west, and the ___E:Miller's River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millers_River_(Middlesex))___ to the southeast. [citation needed]
Land in early Somerville was used primarily as grazing commons and small farms.
After the proliferation of the railroads in the area during the mid-1800s, industrialization transformed the landscape.
In the 1800s, the Millers River was used as a sewer and dumping ground for local industry and would be ordered filled by the Commonwealth before the end of the century, for health reasons.

As a result of landfill and the elimination of former Cobble Hill, the Millers River marsh was turned into ___E:railyards U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railyard)___ , ___E:slaughterhouses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slaughterhouse)___ and other large-scale land uses.

Somerville's commercial property is not concentrated in a recognized downtown ___E:central business district U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_business_district)___ but instead is spread over many different nodes or corridors of business activity.

The difference in character ranges from the vibrant nightlife, live music and theaters of ___E:Davis Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davis_Square)___ to the large scale retail and highway access of ___E:Assembly Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_Square)___ .
This spatial allocation is directly related to the early influence of rail and streetcar systems which caused economic activity to occur at stops.
The other key factor in the creation of commercial squares is the area's topography.
The numerous hills making up Somerville's landscape determined where road networks would allow neighborhood commercial development.

This was especially accelerated by the ___E:dot-com bubble U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot-com_bubble)___ of the late 90s, rising incomes, and concomitant rises in demand for urban housing.

The economic and cultural clash between the city of Somerville and its neighboring cities of Boston and Cambridge has created an underlying tension between residents that has persisted for multiple generations.

Both ___E:Porter Square station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porter_Square_station)___ on the Red Line and Commuter Rail's ___E:Fitchburg Line U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitchburg_Line)___ in Cambridge and ___E:Sullivan Square station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sullivan_Square_station)___ on the Orange Line in Boston's Charlestown neighborhood are located adjacent to Somerville along the border.
Although only 43.6% of Somerville commuters drove alone to work in 2013, several major arteries pass through the city.

___E:McGrath Highway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McGrath_Highway)___ is a major north–south route that represents the portion of ___E:Massachusetts Route 28 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_28)___ through the city of Somerville.

McGrath is the continuation of Monsignor O'Brien Highway in ___E:Cambridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts)___ to the southeast and is known as the Fellsway north of the junction with Mystic Avenue and Interstate 93 in ___E:Medford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medford,_Massachusetts)___ .
The highway has a long and complex history that hints to the changing nature of transportation throughout Somerville and the greater Boston metropolitan region.
Originally constructed in 1928 to create a speedier connection for Route 28 between the Charles and Mystic Rivers, McGrath was elevated in the 1950s to further facilitate increased travel speed.

The result was to cut off ___E:East Somerville U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Somerville)___ and the ___E:Inner Belt District U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Belt_District)___ from ___E:Winter Hill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Hill,_Somerville,_Massachusetts)___ and the rest of the city. When Route 28 was built, its primary purpose was to serve regional commuters traveling into Boston.
However, it soon became clear that McGrath would need to be replaced by a larger and safer highway.

The construction of the elevated ___E:Northern Expressway (Massachusetts) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_93)___ , part of ___E:Interstate 93 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_93)___ , was completed in the early 1970s and essentially rendered McGrath redundant.

Today, the infrastructure of the two raised portions (the McCarthy Overpass, running from Somerville Avenue to Medford Street, and the Squires Bridge, running above the MBTA Fitchburg line near Twin City Plaza) are decaying and decrepit.

In 2013, the Massachusetts Department of Transportation recommended that the McCarthy Overpass that crosses over several streets in Somerville be torn down, and proposed a boulevard-syle reconstruction with bike lanes and sidewalks for pedestrians.
No date has been set for construction to begin.

___E:Northern Expressway (Massachusetts) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_93)___ runs northwest and southeast through Somerville, separating ___E:Ten Hills U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ten_Hills)___ and ___E:Assembly Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_Square)___ from the rest of the city. The massive elevated "Northern Expressway" was completed in the early 1970s and passes directly through Somerville running alongside and/or above Mystic Avenue ( ___E:Massachusetts Route 38 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_38)___ ).

Commonly referred to as the "upper and lower decks of 93", the Somerville-Charlestown section of the Northern Expressway carries three lanes of northbound traffic on the upper deck, and three lanes of southbound traffic on the lower deck. The highway also serves to cut off ___E:East Somerville U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Somerville)___ from ___E:Charlestown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlestown,_Massachusetts)___ .

As of 2010, snow removal from city streets and properties uses 42 pieces of equipment (including front-loaders and plows), about 10,000 short tons (9,100 t) of salt imported from Egypt, and a budget of $500,000.  When the mayor declares a snow emergency that puts special parking restrictions into effect, in addition to electronic media and a press release, a switch at DPW headquarters on Franey Road activates 16 blue lights at major intersections to alert the public.
Two crews of four people (with help from school janitors) clear sidewalks at 33 city-owned buildings.
Excess snow in major pedestrian squares is removed and dumped on a vacant lot on ___E:Winter Hill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Hill,_Somerville,_Massachusetts)___ .
Somerville is considered to be a highly walkable  and bikeable  city. In 2013, 7.8% of all commutes were made by bicycle, ranking Somerville fifth among U.S. cities for its share of bicycling.
In 2013, 49.8% of Somerville commuters either walked, biked or used public transit.
Somerville launched its first ___E:Bluebikes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluebikes)___ (originally Hubway) stations during the summer of 2012 and now hosts 21 stations.

The ___E:Somerville Community Path U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerville_Community_Path)___ is a ___E:mixed-use path U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-use_path)___ that runs along the old ___E:Boston and Lowell Railroad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Lowell_Railroad)___ right-of-way from ___E:Davis Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davis_Square)___ across Somerville to the Cambridge border near ___E:Lechmere Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lechmere_Square)___ .

Roughly 0.8 mi (1.3 km) of the path is finished and in use.  The two finished segments feature pavement interspersed with brick and surrounded by grass, trees, pedestrian connections to nearby streets, and a community garden.
The path is lit at night and snowplowed in the winter.
In 2013, the city broke ground on the first extension in almost twenty years that extended the path another 0.25 mi (0.40 km) east from its then-terminus at Cedar Street to Lowell Street.

Somerville has among the highest bus ridership in the Boston metro area. Nearly 40,000 passengers board the buses that pass through Somerville each day, and 15 ___E:MBTA bus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_bus)___ routes operate in Somerville.
Somerville is protected by the 152 paid, professional firefighters of the city of Somerville Fire Department (SFD).

The Somerville Fire Department currently operates out of five firehouses, located throughout the city, and operates five engine companies, three ladder companies, and one rescue company, commanded by an on-duty district chief and deputy chief each shift.    ___E:Emergency Medical Services U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_Medical_Services)___ have been provided by ___E:Cataldo Ambulance Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cataldo_Ambulance_Service)___ , a ___E:private ambulance company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_medical_services_in_the_United_States#Private/for_profit_EMS)___ , since it was founded as Somerville Ambulance Service in 1977.

The city provides contracted trash, ___E:single-stream recycling U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-stream_recycling)___ , yard waste, and ___E:hazardous waste U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazardous_waste)___ pickup for residents in buildings with six or fewer units,  and ___E:textile recycling U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textile_recycling)___ pickup for all residents.

Single-stream recycling materials are sent to the ___E:Casella Waste Systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casella_Waste_Systems)___ processing facility in neighboring ___E:Charlestown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlestown,_Boston)___ .
